title: Develop your minor pieces first
objectives: Understand why an early queen sortie is risky
Choose a solid developing move over a flashy queen move

steps.text: Moving your queen out early looks aggressive, but it's usually premature. Minor pieces — knights and bishops — can attack the queen for free, forcing it to retreat and costing you tempo while your opponent develops. Bring your knights and bishops out first; the queen joins the game later, once it has support.

steps.prompt: It's early in the game. Which is the stronger opening priority?
options: Bring the queen out to attack right away
Develop your knights and bishops first
Move the same pawn twice in a row

feedback.default: An early queen move usually just gets chased around by minor pieces. Developing knights and bishops first is the stronger, more reliable plan.

steps.successExplanation: Right — developing your knights and bishops first gets your whole army into the game before the queen becomes a target.

steps.prompt: True or false: an early queen move is always a losing blunder.

feedback.default: Not always — but without support from your other pieces, an early queen is usually just a target. It's rarely a game-losing blunder by itself, just an inefficient use of your first few moves.

steps.successExplanation: False — it's not automatically losing, just usually inefficient: you spend moves retreating instead of developing.

steps.summary: Develop your minor pieces before your queen — a queen without support just gets chased around, wasting the moves your opponent uses to develop.
